# Phase 6 — It Is Beautiful

*Goal: the modern high-end renderer. Ordered so that structural changes land before the effects that depend on them.*

> **Every effect in this phase and the next needs an off switch.** The target is a game that scales from "one core while multitasking" to "everything on", which means quality levels are part of each feature's definition of done, not a pass at M34. See "The End Product".

### ✅ M23 — Renderer restructure: PBR and deferred/hybrid · **Core**

Physically based materials (albedo, normal, roughness, metallic, emissive), a G-buffer architecture, HDR rendering and tone mapping.

**Why first in this phase:** every subsequent effect assumes this structure. Retrofitting PBR after shadows, GI, and water exist means rewriting all of them.

**Result**, shipped as six slices (`m23planning.md` has the full plan):

- **M23a — the frame's data.** `FrameUniforms` moved everything constant across a frame out of push constants and into a uniform buffer, one per frame in flight, mapped once. `MeshPushConstants` fell from 144 bytes to **80**, which is well inside the 128 Vulkan guarantees — the device-rejection check that existed because we were over it is gone.
- **M23d — the UI on its own pass** (deliberately before M23b, so bloom cannot bleed off the HUD). `hud.frag` and a pipeline with **no depth attachment at all**; screen geometry is sorted farthest-first by triangle instead. `GraphicsPipeline` took a `PipelineDesc` struct, because there are now seven pipelines and they disagree about nearly everything.
- **M23b — HDR and tone mapping.** The world is lit into a 16-bit floating-point image, blurred into an eight-level bloom pyramid, and squashed back to the screen by one of four curves. **Khronos PBR Neutral is the default** rather than ACES, because ACES hue-shifts saturated primaries and a blocky palette is nothing but saturated primaries. F10 cycles, F11 toggles bloom.
- **M23c — the material table.** One packed word per *texture layer* saying roughness, metallic and emissive, in a storage buffer. Keyed by layer rather than by block, so six hundred stairs and slabs inherit their parent's answer for free. A storage buffer rather than a texture, which sidesteps the trap that every texture here is `_SRGB` and a roughness of 0.5 gamma-decoded is 0.214.
- **M23e — the vertex.** 40 bytes to **32**: colour packed to four bytes, and a new `surface` word carrying an exact face normal in three bits and ambient occlusion in eight. Face shade and ambient occlusion had been multiplied into one unrecoverable float; they are separate facts and are separate now.
- **M23f — the deferred pass.** Opaque geometry writes what a surface *is* into three screen-sized images; one full-screen draw then lights every pixel at once with Cook-Torrance GGX. Sky, water and the block outline stay forward, because a blended normal is not a normal.

**F12 cycles nine surface debug views** — albedo, normal, roughness, metallic, occlusion, emissive, light, distance. That is how a deferred renderer is debugged, and it is what found the material table's two faults.

> ⛔ **The bug worth remembering: the whole world went purple.** The G-buffer shader kept a line multiplying the texture by the vertex colour. For world geometry those three channels are **sky light, block light and face shade**, not a tint — so green was scaled by block light, which is zero away from a torch. The old forward shader had the identical line and then overwrote the result further down, so it had never mattered. **When you move a line into a new shader, check whether the old one later overwrote it.**

### ✅ M24 — Sun, moon, and dynamic shadows · **Core**

Day/night cycle, directional lighting, cascaded shadow maps.

**Result:** the sun casts real shadows, and so does the moon.

**Cascaded shadow maps.** The world is rendered from the sun's point of view into a depth-only image, split into two to four **cascades** — slices of the distance in front of the camera, the nearest small and sharp, the furthest large and coarse. They are layers of one image, so the lighting pass picks between them with an index. `G` cycles quality (off / 1024×2 / 1536×3 / 2048×4, reaching 64 / 128 / 192 metres); `shadows` in `settings.cfg` is the same number.

Three decisions that are not obvious and should not be undone:

- **The shadow pass culls nothing.** Front-face culling is the textbook cure for shadow acne and it is *wrong here*: a voxel mesh is a hollow shell — the mesher never emits the face between two solid blocks — so the far side of a hill does not exist, and front-culling would leave flat ground casting no shadow at all. A slope-scaled depth bias and a normal offset do that job instead.
- **Each cascade is fitted to a sphere, then snapped to whole texels.** A box fitted to the slice changes size as the camera turns, so the map's scale changes with it and every shadow edge in the world crawls. A sphere is the same whichever way you look.
- **One directional light, not two.** Whichever body is above the horizon owns it, so moonlight goes through the same cascades and the night has a lit side and a dark side instead of being a flat wash. The handover at dawn has no step in it because both fade on the same ramp.

**The moon**, eight phases, one texture layer each, advancing a phase per day. The reference draws its sun and moon *additively* against black, and we have no additive pass — so the staging tool derives alpha from brightness, which is what an additive blend does and what gives the crescents their shape for free. Both bodies also switched from our own art to the reference's.

> ⛔⛔ **The sky bodies were reworked on 2026-08-09 and their orientation is NOT settled.** Three fixed and verified: a faint square halo around them (the derived alpha never reached zero — it bottomed out at 14 against a snap threshold of 10, so every texel of the tile stayed slightly opaque); they now sit just inside the far plane instead of at 320 blocks, so they set at the true horizon rather than appearing to sink into nearby ground; and they are exempt from distance fog, which was dissolving them as they set.
>
> **The orientation is the open one.** The player reported them "rotating" and asked for a square that never turns. Four bases were tried, three were rejected, and the fourth is unverified — see the table in `SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` → "Sun, moon and sky". **The two requirements are in genuine tension: "never appears to turn" is only satisfiable by a camera-spanned quad, which is exactly the swivelling-in-world they also rejected. Ask before changing it again.**

**A point light on the camera** was built during M23f and is **off by default**, which is a decision rather than a default value: its light direction *is* the view direction, so every surface faced head-on sits at the peak of its own specular highlight, and it reads as a bright spot glued to the middle of the screen. `handheld_light` turns it on for anyone who wants it.

Release build, render distance 12, shadows on medium:

| | Draws | Triangles | GPU | FPS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| M23 (no shadows) | 121 | 551,289 | 0.46 ms | 121 (capped) |
| **M24 (3 cascades)** | **568** | **3,282,811** | **2.24 ms** | **121 (capped)** |

The extra draws and triangles are the world drawn once more per cascade. GPU time is 2.24 ms against an 8.3 ms budget at 120 fps.

**Also fixed here, from a playtest:** water hanging in mid-air. A probe put it at a 32×2 sheet of water *sources* at y=64 in the chunk at the origin, left behind by a long-deleted test harness that wrote into the real world; generating the same chunk from the same seed produces none of it. **Bumping the chunk format version did nothing, because the file was two versions old and the loader had an upgrade path that accepted it.** Retiring that path is the fix — see `LESSONS.md`.

### ✅ M25 — Sky and atmosphere · **Core**

Atmospheric scattering, sunrise/sunset behaviour, fog and haze, altitude effects.

**First slice shipped 2026-08-09: clouds, a gradient sky, and the lighting round the player asked for after M24.**

**Clouds are raymarched, and their shapes are the reference's.** No geometry at all — a full-screen march through a slab, which is what makes flying through the layer work: no near plane to slice a quad against, nothing to sort, no inside face to vanish. The coverage field is **quantised to the reference's own 12-block cell grid and thresholded hard**, so a cloud is built out of square pieces exactly as the original's is; the volumetric part is only the *shading*, not the shape. Beer's law, a three-tap light march spaced against the cell size, and a Henyey-Greenstein phase with a floor. `C` cycles off / fast / fancy.

**The deck sits at y 140 in a world 96 blocks tall**, and that is not a mistake — a cloud field is a field, not geometry, so it is not bound by the build ceiling. The first attempt put it at 74, where the entire visible sky spanned less than one cloud and the whole thing rendered as a flat white veil.

**Cloud shadows on the ground are six lines and are most of what sells it** — one coverage sample walked from the surface along the sun. A cloud passing over open ground is visible from anywhere; the deck itself needs you to look up.

**The sky is a gradient now, not one flat colour.** It is written by the lighting pass wherever nothing was drawn, so it cost no pass and no geometry. The **horizon is exactly the fog colour** terrain fades to, which is what keeps the join invisible; the zenith is that colour pushed toward blue and darkened; and two glow lobes around whichever body is up give the sun its halo and the sunset its spread.

**Three lighting corrections from the playtest, and the first is the interesting one:**

- **A normal recovered from the triangle always faces the camera**, so every leaf on every tree was lit as though turned toward you and the sun's highlight followed you round the trunk. Cutout faces now carry their real normal and the shader flips it toward the eye.
- **Ambient and direct light are gated differently.** Ambient scales off baked sky light, so a cave is dark. The directional half is gated by the **shadow map**, which can see a hole in a leaf where baked sky light cannot — so sun reaches inside a canopy instead of lighting only its outer shell.
- **Water reflects.** The forward pass carries every surface the deferred one cannot, and water is the whole reason it exists, so the one genuinely reflective thing in the game was the only one never catching the sun. It has a GGX specular and a Fresnel term that takes it opaque edge-on.

**Night is dark now.** Ambient fell from 0.22 to 0.09 and the floor from 0.06 to 0.03; what makes a night navigable is the moon having a *direction*, not the ambient being raised until everything is visible.

**ACES is the default tone curve**, by the player's own choice after comparing all four on screen.

**Closed 2026-08-10 — real atmospheric scattering.** `skyRadiance` was a fog-coloured horizon, a hardcoded blue multiply for the zenith and two glow lobes. It is now single-scattered sunlight: Rayleigh coefficients in the reference's own one-over-wavelength-to-the-fourth proportions, a Mie term for haze, both phase functions written out, and an air-mass approximation that grows toward the horizon. **The sunset is no longer painted on** — light arriving from a low sun has crossed enough air that its blue has been scattered out of it before it gets here, and that is a term in the expression rather than a colour anyone chose.

> ⛔ **The model is applied as a ratio against its own value at the horizon**, never as an absolute radiance. The horizon must stay *exactly* the fog colour or the join with fogged terrain becomes a visible line, and that constraint outranks physical accuracy. Dividing by the model's own horizon value at the same azimuth keeps the join exact and lets everything above it be real.

**Altitude, and it had to be exaggerated to exist at all.** Air thins with height on a 70-block scale, against a real atmosphere's 8,500 m and a world 96 blocks tall — at any honest scale, climbing a mountain here would change nothing. Rain takes the shaping out, because overcast air scatters so many times that the gradient washes into flat grey. **Cloud colour follows the body** rather than a fixed white, so a deck at sunset catches the sunset.

**Night was too blue, and the player said so plainly** — it "gives a false feeling that it's day". Two changes: the night sky colour is a third of what it was and much less blue, and the scattering shaping now fades out with the strength of the light doing the scattering. The moon is a fifth of the sun, so at midnight the sky is very nearly its own flat dark colour and the moon's halo is what lifts it.

Still owed: nothing.

### ✅ M26 — Water as a system · **Core**

Reflection, refraction, depth-based absorption, underwater scattering, waves, foam, shoreline effects. Water is a headline visual feature, not a transparent block.

**First slice shipped 2026-08-09**, from a playtest note that water only ever looked reflective from one particular angle.

**A copy of the lit scene is taken between the lighting pass and the forward pass, and water reflects out of it.** It cannot read the image it is being drawn into, and it must not see itself — so the copy is made after the world is lit and before anything translucent goes in. **Alpha in that image is the pixel's distance from the eye, not opacity**, which is what turns one image into both a colour source and a depth source; nothing downstream reads alpha, and the forward pass overwrites it afterwards. That one decision is what buys reflection *and* absorption for a single full-screen copy — about 0.1 ms — instead of a second depth image and a second set of barriers.

The reflected ray is marched through it in twenty-four lengthening steps and a step counts as a hit when it has travelled further than the surface standing at that pixel. Two limits are real and are faded rather than hidden: **anything off the edge of the screen was never drawn**, so the reflection fades out toward the border and into the sky gradient; and the copy predates the sun, moon and clouds, so those come from the gradient too.

**Reflections are pixelated on purpose** (player instruction). Everything water reflects is worked out from a position snapped to the block texture's own grid — one block face is one texture, so dividing a block by that texture's width gives exactly the grid the rest of the world is drawn on. A smooth mirror in a game made of squares looks borrowed from a different game.

**Fresnel is the physical fifth power and is not a style choice.** Looking straight down a surface returns 2% and you see the bed; a few degrees off the horizon it returns nearly all of it and the lake becomes a mirror. That asymmetry *is* what water looks like, and its absence was the original complaint.

**Depth-based absorption is what stopped the lake reading as tinted glass.** The thickness of water the view ray crosses comes from the same copy, and opacity follows Beer's law through it — clear at the edge where it is an inch deep, solid a few metres out. One flat opacity made ten metres of water exactly as legible as one.

**Ripples, and a surface that moves.** Three crossing sine trains, each shorter, shallower and slower than the last — which is what deep water does, since a gravity wave's speed falls with its wavelength. The **vertex stage displaces the surface and the fragment stage shades it from the same field**, which is why `waves.glsl` exists and has no dependency on anything else: two stages disagreeing about the shape would run the light down the wrong side of every swell. Only vertices the mesher marks as a fluid's top move, so a waterfall's foot and the sides below the waterline stay put and no column can open a seam. `water_waves` and `water_reflection` in `settings.cfg` are the dials.

Also here, from the same playtest: **shadows darken the ambient sky as well as the sun**, `shadow_darkness`, default 0.55. Cutting the directional half is all a shadow map can do on its own and it left shadows reading as pale patches; a point the sun cannot see is also cut off from much of the sky, so this is both the honest answer and the only dial with real range in it.

**Closed 2026-08-10.** **Underwater light shafts**, marched twelve steps along the view ray inside the lighting pass — no new pass, no new target. Each step is sampled against **the same caustic field** that already draws the net on the seabed, taken where a vertical ray from that step would leave the water, so the shafts line up with the pattern on the floor instead of being a second unrelated effect. They taper with depth and are jittered by the interleaved gradient the contact shadows already use, so twelve steps read as grain rather than as twelve bands. This is the one thing that needed a new uniform: being submerged was one bit, which is enough to fog and not enough to know where the light is coming from.

**Ice forms**, on the same pass that settles snow — a water *source* only, under an open sky, with nothing above it and no torch nearby. Freezing a flowing cell would be undone by the next fluid tick and leave the shoreline flickering.

Still owed: nothing.
### ✅ M27 — Volumetric clouds and weather · **Optional**

Volumetric clouds, rain and snow rendering, wind, storms, lightning.

**Shipped 2026-08-09, end to end, after four parallel research passes** — the findings are in `RESEARCH.md` and the reference's own numbers are used throughout.

**Weather is two independent boolean flags with their own countdowns, not a three-way state.** Rain on for 12,000–24,000 ticks and off for 12,000–180,000; thunder on for 3,600–15,600 and off for 12,000–180,000. A thunderstorm is simply both at once, and the thunder flag keeps cycling while it is dry — which is exactly why storms are rare, why one can begin partway through a rainstorm, and why writing it as an enum with transitions would need a probability table that does not exist in the reference.

**Rain and snow are one vertical quad per world column**, built on the CPU in a disc around the camera and rebuilt only when the camera changes column. That single choice answers the hardest question for free: **the quad starts at the top of whatever blocks that column**, so a roof, a cave and an overhang all work with no shelter test anywhere. A screen-space version would have needed the whole heightmap on the GPU to answer the same thing, and would have fought the art direction as well.

The streaks themselves are **procedural rather than a texture**, so they land on the same pixel grid the blocks do. Rain is a short translucent blue streak; snow is a single fully opaque white texel that wanders on two frequencies and is forced bright so a blizzard does not turn grey at dusk. That pair of differences — measured off the reference's own art — carries most of the signal.

**The wind leans the rain, and where it falls.** The lean is a shear of the pattern rather than a tilt of the geometry: a 44-block quad physically leaned over for a gale would swing eight blocks sideways and part company with the column it belongs to.

> ⛔ **The lean has to be a direction in the *world*, not in the quad.** Every quad is turned to face the camera's own column, so a flat slant applied in quad-local space leans a different way for each one — and looking straight up at that reads as the rain spiralling around you, which is exactly how it was reported. The mesh carries the wind's component along each quad, and the shear uses that. The along-quad coordinate is in world units for the same reason.

**Rain lands on water.** Expanding rings, four tiles around the point, each firing on its own offset and dying as it spreads — added to the wave gradient rather than being a normal of its own, so it costs nothing but a few sines and a lake stops being glassy in a downpour.

**What falls is decided by biome**, not globally: a dry or badlands biome gets nothing, and below the reference's own 0.15 temperature it snows, with the temperature falling 0.00125 per block above y 81. Lightning re-checks the same rule, which is why it never strikes a cold or dry biome.

**Lightning is random midpoint displacement**, five generations, three strands, each segment a cross of two quads so it reads the same from every angle without knowing where the camera is. It is drawn white and emissive so bloom gives it a halo — which is what the reference gets from four nested shells blended additively. The flash is **two to four return strokes, not one ramp**: a single fade reads as a camera going off. Thunder follows at `distance / 343`, which the reference does *not* do — it plays thunder to the whole world at once — and is a deliberate divergence.

**The sky, the fog, the sun and the cloud deck all respond, on staggered ramps.** Rain flattens the sky toward grey rather than tinting each biome's own colour, thunder blends three quarters of the way again, the view closes in by about a third, and the sun drops to roughly the reference's 15 → 12 → 10. **Cloud darkness is derived from the deck's own coverage** rather than passed in as a second uniform, because an overcast sky is exactly what a dark deck means and two numbers saying the same thing can only disagree. Coverage runs on a thirty-second ramp against the rain's five, so the sky gathers before the first drop.

`V` cycles rain / storm / clear / back to the cycle; `weather=0` freezes it; `start_weather` opens a world already in one, which is the only reliable way to test it.

**Closed 2026-08-10.** **Wet surfaces darken and shine**: water fills the pores of a surface so less light escapes back out of it, and leaves a smooth film on top, so albedo drops and roughness drops together. Gated on sky light, so the inside of a house stays dry, and snow is exempt because snow does the opposite. **Splash particles land on water** — the rain scatter used to find the highest *solid* block, which is the seabed, so the one splash worth having was the one it could not make. (The ripple rings it was also listed as owing turned out to have shipped with the water work already.)

**Snow accumulates as real blocks.** Seven depths, two texels each, with the eighth being the solid snow cube that already existed — and every one of them draws the snow texture that was already loaded, so the family cost no art, no layer constant and no staging row. Columns near the player are picked on a timer, which is the reference's random tick in everything but name; a torch keeps its own patch clear.

**A bolt does something.** It damages everything in the reference's own box, lights a fire where it lands, and **charges a Bramble** — which is where a charged one is supposed to come from, and which the code had been apologising for in a comment since M20d. The fire is only safe to light because the same storm now puts it out: anything burning under an open sky is extinguished on its next fire tick, which is exactly the pairing the reference has.

Still owed: nothing.

### ✅ M28 — Particles and foliage · **Optional**

GPU-driven particles; dense, animated, wind-affected vegetation.

**Shipped 2026-08-09.**

**Particles are simulated on the CPU, and that is a decision rather than a shortcut.** "GPU-driven" came from a vision document rather than from the player, and a compute-driven system means a storage buffer, an indirect draw, a compaction pass and a second way of getting work onto the GPU — for a few hundred quads that cost microseconds to build. Everything is plain data in one contiguous array with a hard ceiling of three thousand, because the one thing a particle system must never do is spike a frame when something dramatic happens. Revisit it when something needs a hundred thousand at once.

**They need no pipeline of their own.** A particle is a camera-facing quad carrying a quarter of a block's texture, with sky light, block light and a face shade in the same three vertex channels world geometry uses — so it goes down the existing lit, cutout path with no case for particles anywhere in the shader. The quads are built facing the camera on the CPU, which costs two cross products for the whole set rather than a matrix multiply per vertex, and the mesh is rebuilt each frame through the same upload path the HUD has always used.

> ⛔ **They shrink as they die rather than fading.** The cutout path throws a fragment away below half alpha, so an alpha ramp does nothing at all until it crosses the threshold and then blinks the whole particle out at once.

Three things spawn them so far: **breaking a block** throws off a shower of chips of its own texture, **rain landing** makes a fleck of water where the sky can actually reach the ground, and **a hard landing** kicks up a puff of whatever you hit. Collision is a point test against the block grid, one axis at a time, so a chip that hits a wall slides along it rather than stopping in mid-air. A chip rests where it lands rather than bouncing — a bouncing one reads as a dropped item, and there is already a system that looks like that.

**Grass and leaves bend with the wind.** One wind vector drives the cloud deck's drift, the rain's slant and the foliage together, so they cannot disagree about which way the weather is going — something neither the reference nor the well-known shader packs do. The displacement is always *along* the wind and never through zero, because grass bends, it does not wag; a per-position phase stops a field moving in unison and a shared gust makes it occasionally do exactly that. Only the top half of a plant blade moves, so it stays rooted where it was planted.

> ⛔ **The sway flag was tested against the fractional part of a world height that is always integral**, so grass stood perfectly still while leaves moved. A plant blade's corners sit on whole block boundaries; the test has to be against the quad's own extent. Same family as every other bug here where a predicate asked a question whose answer could never be yes.

> ⛔ **The sway flag was tested against the fractional part of a world height that is always integral**, so for two rounds grass stood perfectly still while leaves moved. A plant blade's corners sit at whole block boundaries; the test has to be against the quad's own extent. Same family as every other bug in this project where a predicate asked a question whose answer could never be yes.

> ⛔ **Wind gusts rather than blowing steadily.** Two slow waves multiplied, so the product spends real time at nothing — on a clear day the world stands still and then a gust crosses it. A constant breeze reads as an animation somebody left running, which is exactly how the first version was reported.

> ⛔ **The sway phase must turn slowly across space.** At better than a radian per block, two corners of the same blade land on opposite parts of the cycle and move in opposite directions, shearing the plant apart instead of bending it.

> ⛔ **A leaf block moves every one of its vertices, not just its top.** The displacement is a pure function of world position, so two blocks sharing an edge move identically and the canopy stays watertight. Moving only the tops would tear it open.

`particles` and `foliage_sway` in `settings.cfg`. Measured on release: 120 fps, no change in GPU time.

**Closed 2026-08-10.** A particle gained three fields and the system gained five emitters. **Shade, self-lit and wind drift**: the three vertex channels are sky light, block light and face shade, so a particle has no colour of its own — which means smoke is the white sprite darkened, and a flame is the fire block's own texture lighting itself so it still reads at night, a block away from the torch that made it.

**Torches, fire, lit furnaces and lava smoke.** The emitters near the player are found on a half-second timer and cached, because a torch is a rare block and finding one costs far more than drawing its smoke — a full scan every frame or a random stab that almost always lands on air are both worse. **Eating throws crumbs of the food's own sprite**, on a fixed spacing so the same handful appears whatever the frame rate. **A blast leaves a ball of smoke** scaled by its own power, thrown through the volume rather than off its shell, since a hollow ball reads as a ring the moment it thins.

**Ground cover comes in patches now, not an even speckle.** A flat per-column probability spreads the same plant every N columns across a continent, which reads as noise; one low-frequency field multiplying the density gives thick stands with clearings between them at the same average. Eleven biomes had their density raised, and **the three snowy biomes stop being barren** — their `grassDensity` rows were unreachable, because the branch asked for a grass top and their top block is snow.

> **Potions were on this list and there are none in the game** — no potion item, no brewing, no effect system. That is a milestone of its own, not a particle.

Still owed: nothing.

### ✅ M29 — Post-processing and image quality · **Optional**

Anti-aliasing, bloom, motion blur, depth of field, ambient occlusion passes, resolution scaling, high-refresh-rate support.

**Shipped 2026-08-09.** Bloom and the four tone curves arrived at M23; this milestone added the two that were missing and deliberately declined three.

**Contact shadows, with no pass of their own.** Eight taps in a small screen-space disc off the depth buffer the lighting pass is *already reading*, each rotated by an interleaved-gradient offset so the pattern differs per pixel and banding becomes grain. A proper SSAO pass with a bilateral blur would be better and costs two more images, a second descriptor set and two layout transitions; this is a tenth of the work for most of the effect, and it measured 0.2 ms. It only adds what the mesher's baked occlusion **cannot** know — where a creature's feet meet the ground, where a dropped item rests, where two surfaces meet at a distance no vertex knows about — and it fades out past twenty-four metres, where a screen-space radius covers whole blocks and the result is a smear rather than a corner. `contact_shadows` is the radius in screen pixels.

**Anti-aliasing, run after the tone curve and off by default.** Both halves of that are decisions. It has to run after the curve because a bright pixel next to a dark one is a 40:1 ratio in HDR and about 2:1 once graded, so blending beforehand is dominated by whichever neighbour is brightest and barely moves the edge — which is why the whole grade moved into a `graded()` function the anti-aliaser can run over its neighbours. And it is off because **everything in this game is a hard-edged square**: an anti-aliaser strong enough to soften a diagonal also softens every texel boundary in the world, which is the look rather than an artefact. `anti_alias` from 0 to 1 for anyone who wants it.

**Declined, with reasons.** *Motion blur* and *depth of field* both fight pixel art directly — they exist to hide the sharpness this art style is made of.

**Resolution scaling closed 2026-08-10.** `render_scale`, from 0.5 to 1. **The world shrinks and the interface does not**: every pass up to and including lighting, water and bloom runs at the scaled extent, and the tone map is what stretches it back to the window — so the HUD, the text and the inventory are drawn afterwards at full resolution and stay sharp. That split is the whole reason it is worth having. The extent is rounded to an even number on each axis, because the bloom pyramid halves it and an odd width leaves the first mip half a texel out of step. Changing it does the same work a window resize already does, so it is live rather than restart-only.

> **Measured, and the honest number is small: 2.42 ms at full resolution, 2.14 at 0.75, 2.11 at 0.5.** Verified by probe that the extent really is changing (1280x720 window, 640x360 world at 0.5). The frame here is bound by the shadow pass, which is a fixed size and does not scale at all, and by 2.6 M triangles of geometry — not by pixels. **Scaling pixels only helps a frame that is pixel-bound**, and this one is not yet. It will matter much more once ray tracing lands at M30, which is exactly the kind of work it exists to make affordable.

### ✅ M29b — Distance-tiered rendering, a memory sub-allocator, and a bug sweep · **2026-08-10**

*Because the frame was bound by triangles, and nobody had asked where the triangles were.*

**The measurement came first, and it moved the whole plan.** A temporary probe attributed every triangle the mesher emits: opaque terrain 75.8%, plants 13.7%, cutouts 7.4%, fluid 2.7%. And by height band — **65% of all geometry sits in the bottom 32 blocks of a 96-block world**, on the walls of caves sealed inside rock that can never be seen. Dropping distant *plants* was worth 4.3%. Dropping distant *unlit faces* was worth four times that.

**`detail_distance`** is the setting. Within it, everything as before. Beyond it, terrain only: `isDistantDecoration` blocks are not built, cutout interiors are dropped so a canopy becomes a hollow shell, water stops being displaced so an ocean can finally merge greedily, and **faces that receive no light of any kind are dropped**. Creatures, dropped items, projectiles and falling blocks are culled to the same radius. Setting it to the render distance turns it off, which is what makes it something to compare against.

**It is a rendering tier and nothing else.** Everything out there still ticks, paths, spawns, despawns, breaks, burns and is saved. `SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` → "Meshing" has the three load-bearing details: the tier is an *input* to the mesh job, the boundary has one chunk of hysteresis, and a crossing goes through `invalidateMesh`.

| | fps | GPU | draws | triangles | process RAM |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| render distance 6, off | 428 | 2.11 ms | 532 | 3.03 M | 779 MB |
| render distance 6, detail 4 | **481** | **1.73 ms** | 545 | **2.22 M** | 800 MB |
| render distance 12, off | 282 | 3.45 ms | 1179 | 6.76 M | 979 MB |
| render distance 12, detail 8 | **307** | **3.14 ms** | 1180 | **5.67 M** | 945 MB |
| render distance 16, off | 242 | 4.03 ms | 1544 | 8.82 M | 1140 MB |
| render distance 16, detail 8 | **281** | **3.46 ms** | 1543 | **6.71 M** | 1132 MB |

> **The row that matters is the last one against the third.** Render distance 16 with the tier on is cheaper than render distance 12 with it off — 281 fps against 282 at half again the view, 3.46 ms against 3.45, 6.71 M triangles against 6.76 M. The win was never the frame rate at a fixed distance; it is that you can now see half again as far for the same cost.

**The sub-allocator that had been owed since M4.** Vulkan caps how many memory allocations may exist and the spec floor is 4096; two buffers per mesh reached about three thousand at render distance 12 and went *past* the floor at 16. Buffers now come out of 32 MiB blocks — first fit, coalescing, blocks released when empty. **Measured 3100 live allocations → 26**, with no change to the frame. Buffers only, never images, so `bufferImageGranularity` never enters into it.

**A temporary verification harness, run and deleted.** Every block, item, recipe, species and material cross-checked against the loaded texture array and against the crafting matcher, a slot-operation fuzz over the item multiset, and a proof that the distance tier can only ever *remove* geometry — **far-only vertices 0**, which is what says the world's silhouette cannot change with distance. It found real faults, all of one shape: **a `default:` that returns a real value hides every entry nobody wrote.**

- **Blast resistance answered 6.0 — rock — for two whole table runs.** Sixteen stained glass blocks, every flower in run one, bamboo, sweet berries, glow lichen, sea pickles, four nether plants, an end rod and two torches were all blast-proof. Same shape as the `harvestTier` bug of 2026-08-08, in a different function, twice over — the run-2 branch had its own second copy of the same default.
- **Snow layers had no material family**, so they were lit as stone. That single miss was the entire "315 texture layers claimed by two families" startup warning — which was itself overstating by 45× because it counted claim *events* rather than layers.
- **The snow layer and the snow block were both called "Snow"**, so the catalogue showed one name twice. Now Bedrock's own "Top Snow".
- **`isMetalBlock` matched "Deepslate Copper Ore" and "Block of Raw Copper"**, rendering ore as chrome — against a comment in the same function saying an ore must never be metallic.
- **The snow layer's hardness branch was unreachable**, sitting below the flat-shape rule that answers 0 for carpets; `harvestTool` had the order right and said so.
- **A smoker was mined with a pickaxe and dropped nothing bare-handed**, because `isFurnace` answers for both families and a smoker is wood.
- The block icon's right face was shaded 0.68 against the mesher's 0.72; a landed arrow asked `collisionBoxes` rather than the world-aware form, so a lone pane answered as a full cross; drowning was paced by `kLavaInterval`; the status bars carried their own copy of "twenty".
- **`isFood` and `survival::isEdible` now prove they name the same set at compile time**, which is the cheapest verification available here.

**Follow-up the same day, from a playtest report:** *"detail_distance is working but like kinda... if i fly and then move around, i see plants generating really close to me rather than 10 chunks out."*

Measured with a throwaway world flown across the map at sprint-fly speed: **the closest chunk drawn at the wrong tier reached zero — the one under the player's feet.** The mesh queue is a stack and entries arrive in whatever order the chunk map iterates and light propagation dirties them, so a tier upgrade landed at an arbitrary distance rather than at the boundary. Three fixes:

- **Drain the mesh queue nearest-first** (`nth_element`, linear, once per dispatch).
- **`detailWanted` and `detailBuilt` are separate**, so a re-mesh dropped because a neighbour was missing or the player moved on is recovered rather than leaving a chunk stranded at the wrong tier for ever.
- **`m_pendingMeshSet`** makes queueing O(1); it was a linear search over a queue thousands deep.

Plus `gatherVolume` rewritten to copy **a row at a time into the job's own storage** — it walked cell by cell through three bounds-checked accessors and returned 118 KB by value into a second volume that had also just been zeroed. Afterwards the only chunks at the wrong tier are the ring *at* the boundary awaiting their turn, and the count settles to zero the moment the player stops. The F5 overlay's new `tier lag` row makes that watchable.

> **Choosing the two distances matters more than the code does.** `detail_distance` 10 against `render_distance` 12 is a two-chunk band: it pays the whole cost of re-meshing at the boundary and saves almost nothing. The setting earns its keep when the gap is wide.

**And 552 MB of memory, found by asking where the process's gigabyte and a half was going.** Every sound was decoded up to interleaved stereo `float` and kept for the session — four times what a mono sixteen-bit clip needs, against 497 recordings and eight music tracks. Stored as it arrives now, with the mixer converting on read: **1495 MB → 943 MB, frame unchanged, output bit-identical.**

### ✅ M29c — The content pass: farming, the village blocks, and every container · **2026-08-10**

*Because the next milestone is villages, and a village is built out of blocks that did not exist.*

**752 → 1029 catalogue entries, 596 → 1019 recipes, 1128 → 2223 block ids.** Four rounds of work in one session, each preceded by multi-agent research, and the user's standing instruction throughout was that nothing be simplified: _"why would you simplify stuff? we're not here to do the job improperly."_

**Farming**, which is what a village is for. Farmland at a genuine 15/16 through a new `BlockShape::Tilled`, four crops and two stems keeping their age in the id, nether wart, a composter, bone meal, and trampling as a real probability off the landing. `world/Farming.hpp` owns the reference's own growth chance — `1/(floor(25/points)+1)` over the 3×3 patch — and `World::updateGrowth` samples **per chunk** rather than globally, so a farm does not slow down as render distance grows.

**Four more table runs** (the fourth through the seventh), taking `kExtraBlocks` to **580 rows**: the farm, 125 decoratives, the candles and oddments, and finally the ender chest, cauldron, hopper and stowboxes.

**Every workstation that could be finished honestly, was.**

| Block | What it does now |
|---|---|
| **Doors** ×12 families | 32 states each; both halves placed, hinge stored, swing together, break together |
| **Trapdoors** ×12 | 16 states each, hung in the top or bottom half by where you were looking |
| **Beds** ×16 | Two blocks, **set your respawn point and skip the night**; death returns you there |
| **Candles** ×17 | 1–4 to a cell, lit or not, **light level following the count** |
| **Blast furnace** | A real cooker at double speed, through the new `cookerAt` |
| **Barrel, trapped chest, ender chest** | Real 27-slot containers; the ender chest's slots are the **player's** |
| **Stowboxes** ×17 | 27 slots that **keep their contents when broken** |
| **Hopper** | 5 slots, one item every eight ticks, pushes then pulls |
| **Stonecutter** | One block in, its stairs/slab/wall out, at the reference's rates |
| **Grindstone, anvil** | Repair a pair of damaged items, sharing the smithing screen |
| **Cauldron** | Six levels; a bucket fills or empties it, a bottle takes two |
| **Lectern** | Holds one book |
| **Bell** | Rings |

**The interface went from six screens to eight** — `Hopper` borrows the chest region outright, `Stonecutter` is the only screen where a result slot's *index* means anything. `isContainer(kind)` and `resultSlotCount(kind)` are what the shared code asks instead of naming kinds, which is why both cost so little.

> ⭐ **The decision worth carrying forward: a stowbox's contents ride in `ItemStack::damage`.** It is the one per-stack number every save format and every dropped entity already carried, so contents that travel with an item needed no new field, no format bump and no migration anywhere. A `static_assert` holds the box to a stack of one, because two merging would silently lose one set of contents.

> ⛔ **Two traps paid for in this session.** Widening `isChest` and `isFurnace` each killed early-outs already sitting behind them — a barrel dropped a chest, every smoker was named "Furnace". And the HUD has **two** generated sheets: adding a panel and re-running only one left the game reading new offsets out of an old image, which the user reported as "hotbar is broken".

**Verified:** both presets clean at `/W4`, a 45-second Debug soak with zero validation errors and an empty stderr at 120 fps, 1019 recipes with none broken and none shadowed, and every source file free of byte-order marks and mangled characters.

Still owed: the loom and the brewing stand, which need banners and potions respectively and stay decorative until those exist.

### ✅ M29d — Villages, villagers with trades, and the iron golem · **2026-08-10**

**Everything a village is built out of already existed** — doors, beds, all thirteen workstation blocks, farmland, paths, fences and gates arrived at M29c. What did not exist was the village.

**Placement is the reference's grid plus a jitter, and both numbers are stated in blocks.** ⚠ The reference quotes `spacing` and `separation` in *chunks*, and its chunk is sixteen wide against our thirty-two; writing its 34 into a chunk-counted field would have silently doubled every village distance in the world. `kCellBlocks = 448` and `kSeparationBlocks = 160`, so a village can never be closer to its neighbour than 160 blocks and the type is decided by **one biome sample at the origin**, exactly as the reference decides it. `VillageType` is a **column on the biome table**, which is Bedrock's own 26.0 design — a biome without one never holds a village, and that is the safe default for every biome added later.

**Five types, one set of shapes, five palettes.** Plains, desert, savanna, taiga and snowy, over eleven building silhouettes: three small houses, a medium, a large with a real upper storey and a ladder, a workshop with an open counter onto the street, a library lined with bookshelves, a temple, a farm, an animal pen and the town centre. The palette carries the planks, the log, the stone, the roof, the door family, the bed colour and the lamp — so **fifty-five buildings come out of eleven authored shapes**, which is the same trade `ShapedFamily` made for six hundred cut blocks. Snowy has no architecture of its own; it is taiga with snow laid over everything the sky can see, which is the reference's own arrangement.

**Variation is rolled, not authored.** Each building carries a style word: roof pitched or flat, a stone plinth or not, corner posts, window height and spacing, a chimney, which of the palette's two bed colours, and whether it keeps a crafting table or a trade. Desert roofs are always flat with a parapet, which is what makes that type unmistakable from a distance.

**Houses are rigid and roads follow the ground**, which is the one distinction that decides whether a hillside village reads as deliberate or broken. A building's floor is level with the street outside its own door; the hole underneath is poured with a **circular** platform (Bedrock's shape, not Java's square) and whatever the hill left inside is carved out. A plot that would need more than six blocks of fill or three of cut is simply abandoned. Roads are re-levelled **per column**, become a plank bridge over water, and leave one cell in eight as grass — the reference's own trick, and most of why a street reads as worn rather than stamped.

**A village generates nobody with a trade**, which is the reference's own behaviour and much the simplest thing to build: 5% babies, and of the adults one in ten is a nitwit. Every armourer in the world claimed a blast furnace on its first morning. Claiming runs on Bedrock's own numbers — sixteen blocks out and four up, every three to five seconds, **and a villager with no bed will not take a job**. Four new behaviour rows carry the day: `ClaimPoi` (a producer claiming no controller, like the targeting rows), `Sleep`, `Work` and `Mingle`, driven by the reference's five schedule windows. A villager works the morning, gathers at the bell for two hours in the afternoon, goes home at dusk and sleeps. **`Sleep` sits above `Avoid` on purpose**: the reference gives them priorities 3 and 4, which is why a sleeping villager does not bolt from a zombie at the window.

**Fourteen trades wear fourteen outfits.** The sheet grew 3680 → 4704 rows: the golem's 128 and sixty-four apiece for the thirteen trades and the nitwit, each composited base + biome robe + apron exactly as the reference layers them. Unemployed keeps the plain skin, so taking a job visibly changes a villager.

**The iron golem** is a species row, its own rig from `iron_golem.geo.json`, and a construction check. 100 health, 7–21 damage, and a blow that throws you **3.15× as far and 3.71× as high** as an ordinary one — ratios against Bedrock's own player figures, never the raw numbers, which are in units that mean nothing here. It hunts a new `CreatureTag::Monster`, and **the Bramble is deliberately not in it**: the reference excludes creepers from all four of the golem's targeting rows, and an absent tag says that once where a negative filter would say it four times. A T of iron blocks capped with a carved pumpkin raises one in any of three orientations, and **a golem you built never turns on you** — Bedrock has no anger component on it at all, so that is structural rather than a timer set to zero.

> ⛔ **Two faults the probe found that a build and a soak had nothing to say about.** The workshop's counter runs along whichever wall faces the street, and for two of the four facings that is the same cell the job block sits in — every second shop had a slab where its trade should have been. And the site test was rejecting **79% of every biome-eligible cell** at a roughness of 6; measured, and loosened to 11, villages went from one per 2000 blocks to one per 1450.

**Measured, not assumed:** 81 of 841 grid cells produce a village; 8.2 buildings and 6.2 residents apiece; floor holes 0, hollow-under 0, missing doors 0, blocked doors 0 over a whole generated village. Seven of eight villagers had taken a trade within ten seconds of a village loading.

**Verified:** both presets clean at `/W4`, a 45-second Debug soak with zero validation errors and an empty stderr at 120 fps. `kChunkFormatVersion` 3 → 4 and `kCreatureVersion` 2 → 3, so an already-played world regenerates its chunks and re-spawns its animals.

**Not done, and named rather than hidden:** trading itself (no screen, no offers, no emerald economy), breeding, zombie conversion of villagers, curing, raids, the golem's cracked textures and its poppy-offering pose, and the golem's arms hinging at the body's centreline rather than at the shoulder.

### ✅ M29e — Real block models, and the playtest bug round · **2026-08-10**

**Prompted entirely by the user playing M29d and writing down eighteen faults.** Everything here is a fix; nothing is new scope.

**Seven blocks stopped being cubes.** The bell, the cauldron, the composter, the grindstone, the stonecutter and the brewing stand were full opaque cubes, and the torch and brewing stand were two crossed sheets — a *plant's* shape. `BlockShape::Post` was renamed `Model` and now carries all of them, built from the reference's own `models/block/*.json` geometry: stone posts and a plank bar round a gold bell, a log-legged wheel with stone pivots, a bench with a saw plate standing out of it, a rod in three base plates with three blades, and two hollow tubs with a contents plate inside. A `ModelBox` gained `sideLayer`/`lidLayer` so one block can be painted from several images, and `unmirror` so a texture that marks a world direction is not flipped by the mesher.

> ⛔ **Every one of eleven new model layer constants pointed at a nether plant, and eleven `static_assert`s passed anyway.** `ExtraBlockInfo::layer` is an *offset into the appended run*; `blockTextureLayer` adds `kTableSpritesFirst`. The asserts compared the offset against the offset. A twenty-line startup probe printing the file name at each layer index found it in one run — the brewing stand's rod was a lily pad and the bell was weeping vines. The base is stated once as `kTableLayerBase` and asserted against `kTableSpritesFirst`.

**The freeze was an integer divide by zero.** `craftSlotCentre` does `index % layout.craftSize`, and the stonecutter's `craftSize` is 0. That is a hardware fault, not an exception, so the game stopped dead and exited the instant a stonecutter was right-clicked — and read as a memory leak.

**The door "teleport" could only ever have happened to a thin box.** `blockingPlaneAlong` took the nearest face over every overlapping box, so standing inside a 3/16-thick door leaf and moving picked the plane *behind* you and pushed you out the far side. It now takes the box you are moving from and skips faces already passed.

**Fences were casting hard shadows because they are not on the sky-transparent list.** One line, and every fenced village stopped having black stripes laid beside it.

**The rest, in one list:** a bed grew wooden legs and a mattress raised to y 3–9 (its side texture is a *net* — three 3×3 leg faces packed into rows 13–16, so sampling it as a plain face drew neither); the pillow now lands at the head end on all four facings; landing on one bounces at 66%; doors and beds outline as one unit across both halves; torches select as a stick rather than a cell; leather armour stopped having holes once the untinted `_overlay` layer was composited over the dyeable one; and village torches moved onto stone-and-fence lamp posts at the square's corners and beside each doorstep instead of scattered on the paving.

**One new texture layer, appended at the very end:** `stonecutter_saw.png`. A saw blade is a plane standing out of the bench, so it can be neither the block's `layer` nor its `topLayer`.

**Verified:** both presets clean at `/W4`, a 45-second Debug soak with zero validation errors and an empty stderr at 121 fps, and every model looked at on screen rather than reasoned about.

**The bed's top texture was the one fault left open, and it closed on 2026-08-10.** The user's report was *"there's red near the pillow when it should be on top of the bed at the middle of the bed because blanket is missing there."* The head half's lid rect had been cropped to the pillow, which stretched it over the whole head block and left the blanket nowhere: the bed read as one white half and one red half, with the red starting at the join instead of covering the middle. **Its top is one whole face, not a net** — the reference's `template_bed_head` samples `up` at uv 0,0–16,16 over the entire cell — and the image is pillow in rows 0–7, the shadow the pillow casts in row 8 and blanket in rows 9–15. Restoring the full rect puts the pillow at half a block on the outer end, exactly where `lidTurns` already aimed it, and blanket over the other three quarters.

**Two more reports followed on the same block, and the three are one mistake.** The head's outward end face was half red, because it was being drawn from the long-side image, which is half pillow and half blanket — the reference ships a **separate `bed_head_north.png`**, shared by all sixteen colours and white across the whole mattress band, and that is now the last texture layer. And the head's two legs were invisible, because we stage one side image per half where the reference ships a mirrored pair: the foot's packs its leg faces at u 0–9 and the head's at u 7–16, so reading the foot's corner for both left every bed in the world standing on two legs.

> ⛔ **All four bed reports were rectangles guessed out of the images instead of read from the model that names them.** `template_bed_head.json` and `template_bed_foot.json` state every box's extent, every face's `uv` rect and which texture it comes from — ten lines, already in the repo, answering all four before any of them was filed. Every wrong version rendered something plausible, passed `/W4` clean and soaked clean; only the user's eye caught any of it. **When a block is more than a cube, open its JSON first.**

**Verified:** beds put on screen one per facing, one turned so its head end points at the camera and one seen from behind — pillow at the outer end, blanket across the middle, a white headboard and four legs. Both presets clean at `/W4`, a 45-second Debug soak with zero validation errors, an empty stderr and 101 fps.

**Still unreproduced:** a report that a wooden fence drops a plank — a probe over every fence, wall and gate found `dropForBlock` correct for all of them.

### ✅ M29f — The table sweep, and twenty blocks that were never cubes · **2026-08-10**

**A temporary startup sweep** walking every block, item, recipe and model and cross-checking all of it against the **loaded texture array**. It went from **485 faults to zero** in five passes, and everything it found had been shipping for milestones behind a clean `/W4` build and a clean soak.

**Twenty blocks were full opaque cubes painted from art with real holes in it.** One predicate found every one of them: a face that fills its cell and is not a cutout must have no transparent texel in its art. Being opaque they culled their neighbours' faces; not being cutouts their empty texels drew as black.

> ⛔ **Marking them cutout is only half the fix and the half alone is worse.** The art is transparent where the *model* is smaller, so the holes became gaps — a thirteen-texel end portal frame with a cube-shaped hole above it, which is exactly what the player reported. **Ten of the twenty needed the model, not the discard**, and the reference's own `models/block/*.json` gave every one box for box: the **anvil** and its two damaged forms (a plinth, two narrowing waists and an overhanging top), the **end portal frame** at 13/16, the **enchanting table** at 12/16, the **sculk sensor** at 8/16, the **sculk shrieker**, the **campfire** and **soul campfire** as four logs, **scaffolding** as four posts under a deck, and the **hopper** as a rim, four walls, a funnel and a spout. The **copper grates** and the **spawner** are genuinely `cube_all` and stayed cubes.

**The rest, and none of them was visible from any table:**

- **192 trapdoors stopped sky light dead**, laying a hard black stripe beside every one. `isSkyTransparent` gained fences, walls and gates at M29e and missed trapdoors in the same pass.
- **The cauldron could not be crafted**, because the **compass** had been given its recipe — seven iron in a U instead of four round a redstone — and is declared first, so it shadowed it. The clock had the same wrong shape in gold. The guard that catches this already existed for the generated recipes and had never been run over the hand-written ones.
- **A composter's contents were invisible below level eight.** The plate samples the middle of `composter_top`, which is a rim with a transparent middle; `composter_compost.png` exists in the reference and had never been staged. At level eight the fault reversed — the ready picture is painted *only* in the middle, so the rim drew nothing.
- **A lantern's two handle quads shared a top plane** and flickered where they crossed, and the **stonecutter's saw** took its top edge from an empty row of its own texture.

**The check worth keeping:** for every model box, take the rectangle *and* the layer the mesher will actually use, and assert one texel in it is opaque — side and lid separately, because a net paints them in different corners. That one test caught the bed's invisible legs, the composter twice and the saw.

**Verified:** the ten new models put on screen and looked at, the sweep at zero faults, both presets clean at `/W4`, and a 45-second Debug soak with zero validation errors, an empty stderr and 119 fps. Probe and showcase removed.

### ✅ M29g — Every block measured against its own model, and dropped items stopped being cubes · **2026-08-11**

**Prompted by the player: *"go check every single block against its json file. i think you should be able to code up a script to do it for you."*** Which is the right instinct — the reference ships `models/block/*.json` for everything it has, each naming its elements' `from` and `to` in sixteenths, so the true size of nearly every block we own was already sitting in the repo and nothing had ever read it.

**`block_probe=1` writes `block-shapes.txt` and exits**, one line per block id giving its shape and the box its drawn geometry actually occupies. **`tools/check-models.ps1`** runs that, parses every reference model, and names each block that disagrees by more than half a texel. It is to block models exactly what `worldgen_probe` is to terrain.

**The first run said 175 blocks were wrong. Almost none of them were.** Four corrections to the *comparison* took it to three:

- **A block usually has several models** — a stair is `_stairs`, `_stairs_inner` and `_stairs_outer`, a door is four, a fence is a post and a side. Compare against the first filename that matches and nearly everything reads as broken.
- **A rotation is not a disagreement**, so the comparison runs on sorted extents.
- **A connecting shape must be dumped unconnected**, or a fence in open air is measured against a crossroads.
- **Four families are named differently on each side** — Emberite/netherite, stowbox/shulker box, Bramble/creeper, void pearl/ender pearl.

**Final reading: 2184 blocks drawn, 1293 matched a model and agree, 0 disagree, 888 have no model to check against.** The flower pot was the one real fault it found and it is fixed. Three divergences are deliberate and named in the tool itself, because a *different* disagreement on one of them is still worth seeing: primed **TNT**'s one-texel lift, the **redstone torch**'s painted head, and the **bell**.

> ⛔ **The bell is why "read the JSON" is not always available, and it took three attempts to admit it.** There is no block model for a bell body anywhere in the reference — `bell_floor.json` is the frame alone, because the bell itself is a block entity. So the geometry had to come off the artwork, and every guess at it was wrong in the same two ways: the body shared a plane with the bar it hangs from, and it sampled the transparent column beside its own texture as a stripe down its face. It is five boxes now — two stone posts, a plank bar, a body hanging a hair *into* the bar, and the flared lip — and the player's verdict was *"now the bell finally looks fine."*

**Then the same fault turned out to be everywhere the world could not show it.** A dropped block was **one spinning cube** wearing the block's side texture, so a dropped bell was a gold brick, a dropped torch a cube of torch, a dropped anvil a black cube. A dropped block is now a **miniature of the block**, built from its real boxes with a model's own rectangles and layers. **`iconBoxes` is the single owner of which boxes those are and the hotbar reads the same function**, so the floor and your hand cannot disagree.

> **The 2D sprite path is deliberately untouched**, at the player's instruction: *"it shouldn't apply to objects that have 2d drop sprites."* Flowers, ladders, vines, panes, tools, spawn eggs and buckets stay flat pictures with real thickness. `drop_showcase=1` lays one of every awkward block on the floor with the sprite drops beside them, and saves nothing.

### ✅ M29h — The redstone kit, as blocks · **2026-08-11**

**Forty-one new craftable things and about seven hundred new block states.** Redstone dust, the torch on a floor or any wall, a lever, twelve buttons, fourteen pressure plates, a repeater, a comparator, a piston and a sticky piston with their head, an observer, a dispenser, a dropper, a daylight detector, a lightning rod, a tripwire hook and four kinds of rail. The catalogue went **1030 → 1071** and the recipe table **1019 → 1082**.

**Five research agents went first**, on Bedrock's redstone rules, on the model geometry, and on the three systems still missing (potions, experience, signs and banners). The geometry one paid for itself immediately: **every box here came out of the reference's own `models/block/*.json`**, which is why `check-models.ps1` reads **2448 blocks drawn, 1424 measured, 0 disagreeing** — up from 1293 measured.

> ⛔ **The signal engine is not built, and that is the player's own call:** *"don't do redstone logic — that's too complex and it's like a week worth of work on its own minimum."* Nothing carries power. Every block here places, breaks, crafts, drops and draws correctly and then sits there. Do not start the engine unprompted.

**What Bedrock's arrangement bought us, from the research.** Wire keeps a **strength** and derives its shape from its neighbours, which is sixteen ids against Java's 1296. There is **no quasi-connectivity**. Strong versus weak power is two booleans on a block rather than a level it re-broadcasts. All three are recorded for whenever the engine is built.

**Buttons and pressure plates are `ShapedFamily` rows**, so twenty-six families arrived with no art, no name row, no hardness row, no tool row and no blast row — the same trick that landed six hundred and forty cut shapes in an afternoon. The sixteen wire pictures are the reference's own art **tinted at staging time** by the power they stand for, because the reference tints at draw time and nothing here can.

**Three faults the checks caught before the player could.** The appended target and note-block runs had no texture case and were drawing as **stone** — found by making the material-table warning name the layer instead of counting it. The five shapes you walk straight over (button, plate, wire, rail, tripwire) draw from `collisionBoxes`, which is empty for all of them, so they were **invisible** until `uncollidableDrawnBoxes` gave the mesher and the targeting outline one owner. And `check-models` had to learn that a block **mounted on a wall** is the same shape turned onto another axis, which is nineteen of the twenty disagreements it first reported.

> ⛔ **`blockFacing` was missed for the fourth time, and the player found it:** *"sticky piston has the sticky texture on all sides, it should only be on the push-y side."* The furnace, the chest and the smithing table each taught this once already, and every time **the world was right** — the mesher hands each face a real direction, so the fault lives only in the inventory slot and the dropped item, where an icon draws two side quads and has neither direction to give them. Four `static_assert`s now evaluate the whole expression an icon really evaluates, `blockFacing` and all.

### ✅ M29i — Potions, status effects and brewing · **2026-08-11**

**The thing the documents have listed as owed for three milestones.** There were no potions, no brewing and no effect system at all; there are now a hundred and twenty-four new items and the machinery behind them. The catalogue went **1071 → 1195**.

**`world/Effects.hpp` is the foundation** — header-only, like `Survival.hpp` and `Farming.hpp`, so nothing had to be registered to add it. It carries Bedrock's own effect ids and colours, and **Bedrock's stacking rule rather than Java's**: one slot per effect, a higher strength overwrites, the same strength with longer left overwrites, and anything weaker or shorter is discarded outright. Java hides the weaker effect underneath and hands it back when the stronger expires; Bedrock deletes it, and that is both the reference here and far the simpler thing to store.

> **Three of the formulas are Bedrock's and are not Java's**, which is exactly the kind of thing that would have been wrong if it had been written from memory. Haste is `(1 + 0.2n) x 1.2^n` where Java is flat. Strength is `base x 1.3^n + (1.3^n - 1) / 0.3` where Java adds three per level. Weakness is the same shape with 0.8 and 0.4.

**A hundred and nineteen potions**: forty-one brews, each drinkable and throwable, and thirty-seven of them on the end of an arrow — the four that carry no effect have nothing to tip one with. Their pictures are the reference's own two-layer bottle with the liquid **tinted at staging time** by the effect's colour, one image per brew, which is the same trade the redstone wire makes and for the same reason: the reference tints at draw time and nothing here can.

**Brewing reuses the smithing table's screen**, which the grindstone and the three anvils already do: two things in, a previewed result out. `brewingResult` is a fifty-three row table transcribed from Mojang's own shipped `brew_*.json` files, so the tree is the reference's rather than a reconstruction of it.

> **Two named divergences.** There is **no twenty-second timer and no blaze powder fuel** — both need a block entity that ticks and saves, which is the furnace's entire machinery over again. And water breathing is brewed from a **pufferfish bucket**, because there is no loose pufferfish item in the game to brew it from.

**What the effects actually do.** Milk clears every one of them and dying does too; fire resistance covers lava, fire and burning; water breathing freezes the air bar; speed and slowness scale movement together rather than one replacing the other; regeneration, poison and wither each run on their own cadence, because each one's interval is set by how strong it is. **Poison cannot take the last point of health and wither can**, which is the whole difference between them.

**A glass bottle fills from water** on the same ray the bucket uses — and that one interaction is the only way into the entire tree, because every potion in the game starts as a bottle of water.

### ✅ M29j — Signs and banners, and the blocks the model checker could not see · **2026-08-11**

**Thirty-eight new things**: a sign and a hanging sign for each of the eleven woods, and sixteen banners. The catalogue went **1195 → 1233**, and the recipe table with it.

**None of them needed any art.** A sign is a board of its own planks on a post of the same, and a banner is a sheet of its own wool — so all three families are `ShapedFamily` rows carrying a parent block, and the texture, the tool, the hardness, the blast resistance and whether the thing burns are all forwarded. Their geometry is the reference's own `template_sign_rot_0`, `template_wall_sign` and `template_hanging_sign_rot_0`, box for box.

> **Three named divergences, and the first is the interesting one.** Every wood's sign texture ships at **32x32** and this game's texture array is 16x16 throughout; the honest choices were a second array at twice the size or a downscale, and a downscale is precisely what `make-reference-blocks.ps1` refuses to do. Planks are what a sign is made of and they cost nothing. Second, a standing sign has **four rotations rather than sixteen**, because the box mesher is axis-aligned. Third, a banner carries **no pattern** — the reference has no block model for one at all and composites up to six tinted masks in a block-entity renderer.

> ⛔ **The model checker was skipping every block that collides with nothing.** `block_probe` measured a block from its collision boxes, and a button, a pressure plate, redstone dust, a rail and a tripwire all have none — so all of them fell out of the dump entirely and the previous round's "1424 checked" never included one. It reads from the drawn set now. The same run also taught the comparison two more state suffixes: without `_pressed` and `_down`, a pushed button is measured against an unpushed one and reports a texel of difference that is the whole point of the state.

**The reading at this milestone was 3186 blocks drawn, 1792 measured against the reference's own models, 0 disagreeing** — up from 1424 measured. Signs and banners themselves sat in the unmeasured bucket, because the reference's sign models are thin wrappers the tool did not follow and a banner has no model at all. *(Superseded: the tool has since been taught to follow those wrappers and to count boxes and read `uv` rects, and now reads 3230 drawn / 2629 matched / 0 disagreeing / 271 with no model. It reported **275** disagreeing in between, which is what a checker does when it stops being blind — the current figure lives in `SYSTEM_MEMORY.md`, not here.)*

### ✅ M29k — Thrown potions, and the last hundred and ten entries · **2026-08-11**

**A hundred and ten new things**, and the catalogue reached **1343** — which is **+313 against the 1030 this run started from**, so the "at least three hundred" the user asked for is met with margin. Recipes went 1120 → **1152**.

**Thrown potions finished the brewing work.** A splash and a lingering potion are two new projectile species carrying the brew as a payload, because forty-one of them share two flight paths and the species table has no room for a potion each. Where a splash lands it applies the brew to everyone inside four blocks, weaker the further out they are; where a lingering one lands it leaves a **cloud** that shrinks over thirty seconds and applies a quarter strength once a second. Both are applied in `Main.cpp` rather than in the projectile system, which reads the world and never writes it.

**Then the collectibles.** Twenty-three pottery sherds, eight goat horns, twenty-two music discs and sixteen firework stars. A horn plays one note of eight, low to high, from a single recording at eight pitches — which is the reference's own arrangement, not a shortcut. A disc goes into a jukebox and comes back out of it; a star is a dye burst by gunpowder and a rocket built on one carries the colour.

> **Three named divergences.** The **disc titles are ours** — a track name is expressive work in a way that *stone* and *sheep* are not, so all twenty-two are words we chose. There is **no music**: a disc sounds one note rather than a track, because the music is the one part of this that has to be written rather than reimplemented. And a disc left in a jukebox is **not saved** — it comes back to you when the world reloads.

> ⛔ **Froglights were added twice.** Three enumerators, three table rows, six sprite names and a light-emission branch, all for blocks that had sat in run three since M22. The compiler caught it on the first build, which is the only reason it cost minutes rather than a session — but the rule it broke is the oldest one in this file: **grep every new enumerator name before writing it**, because a block that already exists is not visible from the end of the enum.
